senses.d: During the night following the current day; during the evening of today.
ex: I want to party tonight!
I had a wonderful time with you tonight.

senses.d: Last night.
ex:
I dreamt tonight that I did feast with Caesar,
And things unluckily charge my fantasy;

senses.d: The nighttime of the current day or date; this night.
ex: Tonight is the night.
I have high hopes for tonight.

ety.text: From Middle English tongue, a late spelling of tong(e), tung(e), from Old English tunge, from Proto-West Germanic *tungā (“tongue”), from Proto-Germanic *tungǭ (“tongue”), from Proto-Indo-European *dn̥ǵʰwéh₂s (“tongue”). Doublet of langue and lingua. Cognates Germanic: West Frisian tonge, Dutch tong, Luxembourgish Zong, German Zunge, Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, and Norwegian Nynorsk tunge, Faroese, Icelandic, and Swedish tunga, Gothic 𐍄𐌿𐌲𐌲𐍉 (tuggō).

senses.d: The flexible muscular organ in the mouth that is used to move food around, for tasting and that is moved into various positions to modify the flow of air from the lungs in order to produce different sounds in speech.
ex: But lering and lurking here and there like ſpies,

senses.d: Such an organ, as taken from animals and used for food (especially from cows).
ex: cold tongue with mustard

senses.d: Any similar organ, such as the lingual ribbon, or odontophore, of a mollusk; the proboscis of a moth or butterfly; or the lingua of an insect.
A language.
ex: He was speaking in his native tongue.

[…] that great Towre, which is so much renownd
For tongues confusion in holie writ,

senses.d: The speakers of a language, collectively.
ex: I will gather all nations and tongues; and they shall come, and see my glory.

senses.d: A voice, (the distinctive sound of a person's speech); accent (distinctive manner of pronouncing a language).
ex:
Who are you? Tell me, for more certainty,
Albeit I’ll swear that I do know your tongue.
[...] one of [the prisoners], whom by his tongue I knew to be a Scotchman, lamented most piteously [...]

senses.d: A manner of speaking, often habitually.
ex: She can have a sharp tongue when she's annoyed.

Al maters wel pondred and wel to be regarded,
How ſhuld a fals lying tung then be rewarded?

senses.d: A person speaking in a specified manner.
ex: I know that we must keep apart for a long while; cruel tongues would force us apart, if nothing else did.

senses.d: The power of articulate utterance; speech generally.
ex: I was so overwhelmed my tongue deserted me.
Parrots imitating Human Tongue

senses.d: Discourse; the fluency of speech or expression.
On a wind instrument, to articulate a note by starting the air with a tap of the tongue, as though by speaking a 'd' or 't' sound (alveolar plosive).
ex: Playing wind instruments involves tonguing on the reed or mouthpiece.

senses.d: To manipulate with the tongue.
ex: [T]he cattle tongued at the damp grass, licking rather than grazing. […]

senses.d: To lick, penetrate or manipulate with the tongue during flirting or oral sex.
ex: Hot I tongued her. She kissed me. I was kissed. All yielding she tossed my hair. Kissed, she kissed me.
I was tonguing her ear and serenading her in a passionate whisper, mimicking Elvis, mimicking Joey.

senses.d: To protrude in relatively long, narrow sections.
ex: a soil horizon that tongues into clay

senses.d: To join by means of a tongue and groove.
ex: to tongue boards together

senses.d: To talk; to prate.
To speak; to utter.
ex:
’Tis still a dream, or else such stuff as madmen
Tongue and brain not;

senses.d: To chide; to scold.
ex: How might she tongue me!

senses.d: To flense

From earlier lengua, from Latin lingua.

Any large, excessive, or overwhelming amount of anything.

From Middle English ton, tone, from Latin tonus (“sound, tone”) (possibly through Old French ton), from Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos, “strain, tension, pitch”), from τείνω (teínō, “to stretch”). Doublet of tune, ton, tonos, and tonus.
From Middle English tone, ton, toon, from the incorrect division of thet one (“the/that one”). Compare Scots tane in the tane; see also tother.

senses.d: A specific pitch.

The character of a sound, especially the timbre of an instrument or voice.

A whining style of speaking; a kind of mournful or artificial strain of voice; an affected speaking with a measured rhythm and a regular rise and fall of the voice.

senses.d: The manner in which speech or writing is expressed, especially the aspects of diction (word choice), connotation, emotiveness, and register.
ex: Their tone was dissatisfied, almost menacing.

senses.d: State of mind; temper; mood.
The shade or quality of a colour.

senses.d: The favourable effect of a picture produced by the combination of light and shade, or of colours.
